results.content:
History. See every run and job, where it ran and how long it waited. A failed job shows the failing step, its log and whether a re-run will likely help.

A failed job in History: it failed at Run pnpm check, looks like a type error that a re-run won't fix, with the log excerpt and step times.

Performance. Compare how long jobs take on each runner.

The Performance page's runner table: jobs, median wait and run time per runner, with a MacBook Pro 2.7 times faster than ubuntu-latest.

Signals. Find what makes your CI slow or costly, such as long runner waits and flaky jobs.

The Signals page: jobs waiting for a runner, the job that finishes last, and flaky jobs with the minutes they cost. [...] GitHub Actions jobs go through relayrunner to the first free runner in your order: your machines, self-hosted runners, Blacksmith, then GitHub-hosted.

Route GitHub Actions jobs to the runners you already have.

Install the GitHub App  ·  Dashboard  ·  Website  ·  Quickstart  ·  Docs

Each job goes to the first runner in your order that can take it right now: one of your own machines when it's online and free, an existing self-hosted runner, a hosted provider such as Blacksmith or Depot, or GitHub's hosted runners. You keep your usual push workflow and see the same checks and logs in GitHub. [...] ```
   jobs: relay-test: uses: relayrunner/actions/.github/workflows/relay.yml@v1 with: machine: self-hosted # any connected machine github: ubuntu-latest # used when no machine is free test: needs: relay-test runs-on: ${{ needs.relay-test.outputs.runner }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: npm test
   ```
   
   The relay job gets its answer in about a second and bills no minutes. If nothing fits, it fails with the reason instead of leaving the job queued.

results.content:
AI slop is strong with this one... I saw "per-runner swap" and I was wondering how it's implemented, given that Linux did not support swap partitioning last time I've checked Turns out it's just a lie. The script creates a swapfile per runner, but then merges them all into one big happy system pool, where every swapfile is shared between every runner. | | | |  |  |  |  ---  |  |  | bzmrgonz 69 days ago  | prev | next (javascript:void(0))   I had a different plan in mind, keep everything in cheap s3, save a declarative script on a public repository that deploys forgejo and harbor containerized on the local ephemeral Origin/cache and pull heavy sources and code from s3. | | | |  |  |  |  ---  |  |  | fuck-the-system 67 days ago  | prev | next (javascript:void(0))   I am using ci runners [...] 1. OOM. A memory-constrained box running a couple of heavy jobs at once just gets its builds OOM-killed, silently, and you spend an afternoon blaming flaky tests. Fix: give the box swap — specifically one swapfile per runner — and set vm.swappiness=10 so it only leans on swap under real pressure. Swap isn't the hot path; it's the airbag.

2. "No space left on device" — but the disk looks half empty. The culprit was /tmp silt: dead job-workspace directories that never get cleaned up, slowly filling the disk until a big build tips over. Fix: give each runner its own /scratch (so they don't fight over one /tmp), and add a systemd-tmpfiles rule that ages /tmp + scratch every 6h. Set-and-forget. [...] 1. OOM.
